en: Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Whether one is a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant,"
Whoever desires to attain perfection,
which deity should he worship? For how could there be certain heaven for him [if he does not]?
Whence comes the supreme beatitude?
By what ritual should one offer oblations to the gods and likewise to the ancestors?
And once liberated, what destination would he go to? And what is the nature of liberation itself?
Furthermore, having gone to heaven, what would he do?
By whom one does not fall from heaven; who is the god of the gods,
and likewise the father of the ancestors?
"Therefore, O Grandfather, tell me that which is even higher than that. Bhīṣma said:
"O sinless one, you who are skilled in questioning, you ask me here about a profound matter;
for this cannot be understood through mere reasoning."
It cannot be told even in hundreds of years,
O King, except through the grace of the gods or by means of the acquisition of knowledge.
"For this narrative is indeed profound;
it must be explained by you, O slayer of enemies.
In this regard, they also cite this example:"
This is an ancient history,
a dialogue between Nārada and the seer Nārāyaṇa.
For Nārāyaṇa, the soul of the universe,
the eternal one who exists in four forms,
was born as the son of Dharma.
My father spoke thus to me:
"O Great King, in the Kṛta Yuga, formerly during the Svāyambhuva interval."
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as Hari and Kṛṣṇa— from among them, [the first two are] Nārāyaṇa and Nara.
Having reached the hermitage of Badarī, the two immutable ones performed austerities in a golden chariot.
For that vehicle has eight wheels,
is yoked by the elements, and is delightful;
therein dwell those two, the first Lords of the World.
Emaciated and covered with visible veins,
they were difficult to behold even by the gods, owing to their asceticism and spiritual splendor.
He upon whom they bestow their favor is worthy to behold the two gods;
surely, it must be with their consent.
Impelled by love within his heart,
he descended from the peak of Mount Mahāmeru toward Gandhamādana.
Nārada, a being of great power,
was wandering through all the worlds;
O King, he arrived at that place.
The swift traveler reached Badarī-āśrama;
at the time of their daily rites,
curiosity arose within him.
This is that entire abode in which the worlds,
together with the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, are established.
The *sarṣikī*, *kiṃnara*, and *lelihā*—
this single form was previously born, and it has now become fourfold.
The lineage of the Dharma has been greatly increased by these;
oh, how truly favored we are today!
The Dharma was established here by these gods,
as well as by Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
and likewise by Kṛṣṇa Hari.
In that regard, Kṛṣṇa and Hari,
for some particular reason,
remained there, for they are both preeminent in righteousness.
Likewise, these two are established in austerity;
for they are the supreme abode—
what daily ritual could there be for them?
The parents of all beings are illustrious deities;
which deity, indeed, do they worship?
"Which ancestors [should I honor]?"—
thus he reflected in his mind with devotion toward Nārāyaṇa.
Then,
when the rites for the gods and the ancestors had been performed, it suddenly appeared in the presence of the two deities.
Then he was gazed upon by those two and honored according to the prescribed rite as taught in the scriptures.
Having seen that great marvel and the unprecedented extensive ritual,
he sat down nearby, well-pleased.
The venerable sage Nārada,
having gazed upon Nārāyaṇa with a serene inner soul, [spoke].
Having paid homage to Mahādeva,
he spoke these words:
"In the Vedas, together with the Purāṇas..."
You are sung of in the primary and secondary limbs [of the Veda];
you are the unborn, eternal Creator, considered the supreme nectar.
The past and the future,
this entire world, is established in you,
O God; for the four stages of life (āśramas) likewise depend upon you.
All [duties] are rooted in the householder's life;
day after day, they worship you,
who are established in various forms.
The father and mother of the entire world are the eternal teachers;
which god, then, do you worship today?
Whom do we not know as our father? [X T G1-3.6 M1.5-7 insert: O highly fortunate one, whom do you worship?
Tell that to me who asks you here.]
The Blessed Lord said: This which must be spoken is unspeakable;
it is the eternal secret of the Self.
O Brahmin, because you are devoted to me,
I shall explain to you exactly as it is that which is subtle and unknowable.
It is unmanifest, immovable, and eternal;
it is devoid of the senses, the objects of the senses, and all elemental beings.
For he is the inner self of all beings and is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
he is distinct from the three qualities (guṇas).
And the Puruṣa is likewise conceived;
from him, O best of the twice-born, the Unmanifest (avyakta) was produced, which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa).
That which is unmanifest, yet exists in the state of manifestation—
that imperishable *prakṛti*—
know that to be our common womb.
For he who consists of both being and non-being is indeed worshipped by us both in rites ordained for the gods and for the ancestors.
"Therefore, there is no other superior to him— neither a father, nor a god, nor a twice-born brahmin;
for he is to be known as our very self."
Therefore, let us both worship him;
by that act, O Brahmin, this world-sustaining boundary has been established.
"Rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors must be performed"—
this was his instruction.
Brahmā, Sthāṇu, Manu, Dakṣa...
Bhṛgu, Dharma, Tapas, and Dama; Marīci, Aṅgiras, and Atri;
Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Vasiṣṭha and Parameṣṭhin, Vivasvat and Soma, and also he who is called Kardama.
And Krodha was indeed sold;
thus twenty-one were born,
who are remembered as the Prajāpatis.
They constantly honor the eternal ordinance of that god, as well as the rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors.
Having understood that in its true essence,
those best of the twice-born then know [them] as having attained the Self.
Even those embodied beings who dwell in heaven pay homage to him;
through his grace, they attain [liberation].
They attain the destination ordained by that [action],
those who are deficient in the seventeen qualities as well as in their actions.
Having abandoned the fifteen kalās, they are liberated; this is the certainty.
O Brahmin, such is the destination of the liberated.
He is conceived as the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña);
for he is indeed all-pervading and is described as being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
It is perceived through the yoga of knowledge,
and from that we two have emerged;
having thus known that Self.
We worship the Eternal One,
whom the Vedas and the stages of life (āśramas), abiding in various forms, likewise honor.
They worship the Primordial One with devotion,
and He grants them their goal.
But those in the world who are permeated by that [devotion]—
Established in single-minded devotion,
this is what is superior for them:
that they enter into him.
Thus, O Nārada, this summary of the secret teachings has been proclaimed to you out of devotion and love, O brahmin-sage.
"And it has been heard by you through devotion to us.
Bhīṣma said:
"Thus addressed, that best of bipeds—"
Nārāyaṇa,
the Supreme Person, spoke these words to Nārāyaṇa, the best among bipeds, who dwells for the welfare of the world.
That purpose for which your birth from the Self occurred here,
that supreme [purpose] manifested in four ways within the House of Dharma—
let that be accomplished today for the benefit of the world.
"I go now to behold your primordial nature. O Lord of the World, the Vedas have been well-studied by me; austerity has been practiced, and never before have I spoken an untruth."
I constantly pay honor to my gurus; I have never before disclosed the secrets of others. The four secrets have been guarded by me according to the tradition.
I am always equal toward both enemy and friend; I have constantly taken refuge in that Primordial God and choose him eternally with single-minded devotion.
"With these qualities, my being is completely purified;
why then should I not behold the infinite Lord?
Having heard those words of Pārameṣṭhya, [he spoke].
Nārāyaṇa, the protector of the Sātvata dharma: [X M5 ins:: Therefore, O Lord, grant me your permission;
having seen him, I shall have fulfilled my purpose.]
Having honored him with rites appropriate for his own status, he said to Nārada, "Go. Then,
dismissed by him, the son of Parameṣṭhin departed.
Having paid homage to that ancient seer, he leapt into the sky with supreme speed; then,
he suddenly alighted upon Mount Meru.
There the sage remained for a moment;
having reached a solitary spot on the mountain peak,
he gazed toward the north-west.
And he beheld one endowed with an exceedingly wonderful form. For to the north of the Ocean of Milk lies an island, vast and renowned by the name Śveta.
Indeed, that [mountain] is described by the wise as being thirty-two thousand yojanas high above Meru; and there,
they are beyond the reach of the senses and free from hunger.
Free from movement, exceedingly fragrant,
white, and men who have departed from all evil;
they are the stealers of the sight of men who commit wicked deeds.
Their bodies are of adamantine bone, equal in measure and proportion;
they possess divine lineage and form, endowed with the essence of purity;
their heads are shaped like parasols, and their voices resound like the roar of massed clouds.
They possess four excellent lotuses as their feet, with hundreds of lotuses upon them;
they are endowed with sixty white teeth and eight tusks.

Those who, with their tongues, lick from all sides the face of the god—who resembles the sun and has arisen from the universe—with devotion; //12322.11// [they attain the highest state]. //12322.12//1//
Since all worlds are born from him,
the Vedas, the dharmas, the peaceful sages,
and all the gods are his emanations.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: They transcend the senses, they do not consume food, they are motionless, and they are fragrant.
How were those persons born?
What is their supreme destination— those who become liberated here in this world?
O best of the Bharatas,
this indeed is the characteristic of those men who dwell in Śvetadvīpa.
Therefore, sever my doubt,
for my curiosity is great;
for you are the delight of all discourse.
"And we have indeed taken refuge in you.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, this story is very extensive."
I heard this in the presence of my father;
indeed, it must be told to you,
for it is remembered as the very essence of all narratives.
[X T G1-3.6 M6 Kumbh..ed. insert: Nārada, the best of sages, related this to Śāntanu;
having been questioned by the king in the past, he spoke.]
In this regard, I have heard from the past:
there was a sovereign of the earth named King Uparicara.
He was renowned as a friend of Indra,
a devotee of Nārāyaṇa Hari, righteous, and eternally devoted.
By constantly serving his ancestors without weariness,
he attained universal sovereignty in the past through a boon from Nārāyaṇa.
Adopting the Sātvata ritual,
he worshipped the Lord of Gods, [the mantra] which had previously issued from the mouth of the Sun.
With what remained from that, he shared with his ancestors; with what remained of the offerings to the ancestors, he shared with the Brahmins and his dependents.
Eating only the remnants of food, devoted to truth,
non-violent toward all beings—
he is a devotee with his whole being.
Janārdana, the God of gods,
who is without beginning, middle, or end.
O crusher of enemies, he bore devotion toward that Nārāyaṇa, the imperishable creator of the world.
Śakra himself, the king of the gods, gave him a single bed and seat,
as well as his own self, his kingdom, and his wealth.
Wives and vehicles—
all this belongs to the Blessed One;
thus was it always observed.
All sacrificial rites— whether performed for specific desires, for occasional occasions, or as constant obligations— are supreme acts when one abides in the Sātvata path.
With a concentrated mind, he performed the ritual in the house of that great-souled one, where the foremost experts in the Pañcarātra were present.
The Blessed One has declared that they attain a noble death and partake of the first-fruits of food while he rules the kingdom.
For those who destroy their enemies through righteousness,
no false speech arises,
nor does the mind become corrupted.
And he did not commit even the slightest evil with his body. For those who are renowned as sages—
The seven Citraśikhaṇḍins,
having become of one mind,
proclaimed that supreme scripture.
[The editions of X, K6.7, Bo.6-9, Da3..a4, Dn1.ṇ4, Ds, D2.3.4.5.8.9, M1.5-7, and Ca insert:
It was composed on the great mountain Meru, equal to the four Vedas.
[He] emitted from his seven mouths the unsurpassed Dharma of the world:
Marīci, Atri, and Aṅgiras.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
and the highly resplendent Vasiṣṭha—
these are the Citraśikhaṇḍins.
For these are the seven primary natures,
and Svāyambhuva is the eighth;
by these the world is sustained.
From them the scripture has emerged:
"The sages, with one-pointed minds, self-controlled, delight in restraint."
[They are] knowers of the past, the present, and the future;
they are devoted to truth and righteousness.
"This is the highest good; this is Brahman;
this is the unsurpassed benefit," having reflected thus upon the worlds with his mind.
Then they composed the treatise; therein dharma, artha, and kāma were indeed treated first,
and liberation (mokṣa) was proclaimed last.
And various boundaries established both in heaven and on earth were attained by propitiating the God through austerity.
For a thousand divine years, all of them together with the sages [worshipped] Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord.
For at that time, Sarasvatī, the goddess who instructs Nārāyaṇa,
entered into all those ṛṣis.
Out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
it was then correctly set in motion by the twice-born who were knowers of austerity.
Regarding word, meaning, and reason—
this [grammar] was born at the beginning of creation;
for that treatise existed indeed from the very start.
Adorned with the sound of the syllable *oṃ*,
it was meditated upon there by the sages,
for that is where the Compassionate One dwells.
Then the Blessed One, his body remaining unmanifest, was pleased and spoke to all those seers.
The Supreme Person is invisible. Indeed, this excellent work consists of one hundred thousand verses.
Because from this Dharma proceeds the entire course of worldly affairs,
both in their engagement and in their cessation.
This shall be the source,
honored by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman Vedas,
as well as by the Atharva-Āṅgirasa.
In that same manner, O Brahmins, Brahmā was created by me from my grace, and Rudra was created from my wrath.
You are likewise the primary elements;
the sun and the moon, the wind,
the earth, the waters, and fire as well.
And all the hosts of constellations,
as well as that which is designated as spirits,
abide within their respective offices.
Just as all those who discourse on Brahman are authoritative each according to their own [tradition],
so too is this supreme scripture.
This shall indeed be authoritative;
this is my instruction.
From this, the Dharmas will be proclaimed.
Manu Svāyambhuva himself,
as well as Uśanas and Bṛhaspati,
when they are born.
Then they shall proclaim the treatise extracted from your own insights regarding the duties pertaining to the self-existent [Manus].
And in the treatise composed by Uśanas,
as well as in the doctrine of Bṛhaspati,
which has been thoroughly examined throughout the worlds.
This treatise was composed by you;
from it, Vasu became a protector of his subjects,
indeed through the presence of Bṛhaspati.
O best of the twice-born, he shall attain it;
for that king will be imbued with my nature and will become devoted to me.
By means of that treatise, he will perform all activities in the worlds;
for this is [the essence] of all treatises.
This treatise is designated as supreme;
it is conducive to worldly prosperity and righteousness,
and it is the highest source of renown.
And because he shall set this in motion,
you will become possessed of offspring;
and that king shall be endowed with glory.
He shall become a great lord of wealth. But when that king has passed away, this eternal scripture [shall endure].
"That shall disappear; this is the truth.
This much has been told to you by me. Having spoken these words, [he remained silent].
The invisible Supreme Person,
having dismissed all those sages,
set out toward some unknown direction.
Then those fathers of the world,
who contemplate the welfare of all worlds,
set forth that treatise.
The eternal source of dharma,
when the lineage of Aṅgiras had arisen in the first conceived age.
Having established the scripture, including its limbs and secret doctrines, with Bṛhaspati,
they departed for their desired destinations.
Having resolved upon asceticism for the sake of upholding all worlds,
they are the promulgators of all dharmas.
Bhīṣma said: Then, when that great kalpa had passed and a son had been born to Aṅgiras, [the world was restored].
The gods became filled with joy when the priest of the gods was born;
[they proclaimed] "Great is Brahman! Mighty is he!"
These words are synonyms;
O King,
the learned Bṛhaspati is endowed with these qualities.
He had a preeminent disciple,
King Vasu Uparicara,
who at that time had studied that treatise.
Born from the illustrious Citraśikhaṇḍin;
that King Vasu had previously been purified by divine ordinance.
He protected the earth just as Ākhaṇḍala protects the heavens.
He had a great sacrifice.
The horse sacrifice of that great-souled one had Bṛhaspati as its officiating priest;
he served there as the Hotṛ.
And here, the three sons of Prajāpati became the assistant priests (sadasyas): Ekata,
Dvita, and Trita.
And the great seers Trita, Dhanuṣākṣa, Raibhya,
Arvāvasu, and Parāvasu.
The seer Medhātithi, and the great seer Tāṇḍya;
the illustrious seer Śakti.
Likewise, he who is Vedaśiras,
and Kapila, the best of sages,
the grandfather of Śālihotra.
The first were Kaṭha and Taittirī;
then the elder brother of Vaiśampāyana,
Kaṇva, and Devahotra.
These sixteen have been proclaimed;
all the requisites were gathered for that great sacrifice, O King.
No slaughter of animals took place there;
the king remained thus established—
non-violent, pure, and noble.
Praised for his action free from desire,
he sang the words of the Āraṇyaka;
the portions were prepared there for him.
Then the Blessed One, the ancient God of gods, being pleased with him,
revealed himself directly to him.
Being invisible to anyone else,
he himself smelled the portion and took hold of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
"A portion has been carried off by the invisible god Harimedhas.
Thereupon, Bṛhaspati became enraged.
Raising the *sruva* ladle with impetuous force,
he struck at the sky with its falls;
out of rage, he shed tears.
And he said to Uparicara:
"This portion has been prepared by me;
it must indeed be accepted by the god himself."
This is before my very eyes, there is no doubt;
for the portions of the sacrifice have indeed been received here directly by the gods.
"For what reason has that all-pervading Hari not come here to grant us his vision? Then he [the Lord] addressed him who had thus been agitated.
The great king Vasu, the protector of the earth,
together with all those members of the assembly, propitiated the sage.
[X T G1-3.6 Kumbh... ed. insert: Upāricara Vasu said:
"The portion of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) that has been offered by you here is as much as it is. ]
"O Vasu, this [weapon] was taken by the God of Gods in my very presence; of this there is no doubt. Thus was he addressed by Vasu.
And the preceptor, filled with wrath, said:
"O sinless one, since I have been insulted by you, I shall not perform the sacrifice here."
By you the animal was spared;
a dough-effigy was made [in its place].
You behold the deity constantly.
"How might I not see [this]?
Vasu replied:
"The slaughter of animals has been forbidden."
By means of mantras from the Yajurveda and other sources,
I shall not indeed prevent the act of violence;
I shall behold Hari with single-minded devotion.
"Therefore, you, my elder, must not be angry with me. Bhīṣma said:
But Bṛhaspati, becoming truly enraged at Vasu as he spoke thus,
spoke [in turn] to the sacrificial priests.
"What is our task? he asked, as he restrained them.
Then the great seers Ekata, Dvita, and Trita [spoke].
And they spoke to him, unperturbed:
"You ought not to give way to anger.
Listen, my son, to our words."
"This which we have declared was not the dharma in the Kṛta Age— that you should have harbored such anger."
For that god is free from anger,
to whom this portion has been offered;
he cannot be seen by you.
Or by us, O Bṛhaspati;
whoever he grants his favor to,
he indeed is worthy to see him.

"Those who were one, two, and three spoke; thereafter, they were the Citraśikhaṇḍins. (12323.18808)]
Ekata, Dvita, and Trita said:
"We are indeed the sons of Brahmā, celebrated as his mind-born [sons]."
For they have indeed departed toward the northern direction for the sake of the supreme good,
having performed austerities for thousands of years.
The four [types of ascetics] practice the supreme austerity: standing properly on one foot, motionless as a log, and composed in meditation.
But on the northern side of Meru,
along the shore of the Ocean of Milk,
is that region where we have not been scorched.
"How may we behold the god Nārāyaṇa through most rigorous austerity? [they asked].

To him who is most excellent and the giver of boons.]
To the eternal God of gods,
at the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the vow,
an incorporeal voice spoke.
[With a voice that was smooth and deep, O Lord, which caused great joy.]
"O Brahmins, you have well-performed your austerities with a serene inner self; you are devoted seekers of knowledge."
How will you see that Lord? To the north of the Ocean of Milk is the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), which possesses great radiance.
There, the human beings are devoted to Nārāyaṇa, possess the luster of the moon, and have attained a state of single-minded devotion.
Those devotees enter the eternal god, the thousand-rayed Puruṣottama.
Beyond the senses, free from food,
motionless, and fragrant—
those men are devoted solely to the One.
O sages who dwell on Śvetadvīpa, go there;
it is there that my self is revealed.
Then, having heard that incorporeal voice, we all [proceeded] by the path as it had been described.
They reached that region;
having arrived at the great White Island (Śvetadvīpa),
their minds were fixed on it and they were eager to behold it.
[All were suddenly struck down, bewildered by his splendor.]
Then he came within the range of our vision;
at that moment, he was struck down,
and we did not see the man.
Our vision was stolen by that splendor;
then, there arose in us a consciousness born of divine yoga.
It is said that he cannot be seen directly by one who has not performed arduous austerities;
therefore, once again for a hundred years, [he practiced].
Having performed a great penance for that duration,
at the conclusion of their vow, we beheld most auspicious men.
White, resembling the moon,
and endowed with all the auspicious marks;
they stand with their hands perpetually joined in reverence toward Brahmā.
For those reciting while facing east or north,
that recitation is called "mental";
it is what is recited by those great-souled ones.
By that state of one-pointed mind, Hari indeed becomes pleased; such,
O tiger among sages, as it may be.
The radiance of each individual human being was like the splendor of the sun at the end of an aeon.
"We thought that island was the abode of splendor; indeed, we believed there was no one superior to him there."
All of them possess equal splendor. Then, [one perceives] the radiance of a thousand suns rising simultaneously.
"Suddenly we have seen him once more, O Bṛhaspati! they cried,
and together they rushed forward.
Then those men, quickly with palms joined in reverence, being joyful, spoke only the word, "Homage!"
Then, as they were addressing one another,
we heard a great sound:
"It seems that the tribute is being presented."
By those men, [the state of] that god [was described];
but we, our minds suddenly snatched away by his splendor, [were unable to perceive it].
We do not perceive anything at all, for the power of our vision and our faculties have been destroyed;
yet, a single sound continues without ceasing.
We have heard it uttered,
filling the entire sky and endowed with the phonemes of the *śikṣā*.
Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one!
Homage to you, O creator of the universe!
Homage be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa!
"O Forefather of Great Beings"—
this was the sound we heard,
uttered with the articulation of the syllables of training.
In the meantime,
a pure wind, carrying all fragrances,
blew divine flowers.
And likewise medicinal herbs suitable for ritual action; by those men who knew the five times and were devoted to Hari alone, Hari was worshipped.
Surely the Lord has arrived there,
since such words have been uttered by them.
"Endowed with supreme devotion through our thoughts, words, and deeds at that time,
we nevertheless do not see him."
They were deluded by his illusory power; and when the wind had ceased and the sacrificial offering had been presented, [the gods departed].
"O best of the Aṅgirases, our minds have become agitated with anxiety among these thousands of human beings."
Among those of pure birth,
no one at all honored us with either thought or sight.
Those hosts of sages, established in their own state and devoted to the single reality,
did not direct their thoughts toward us.
Having been established in the state of Brahman, [they said:
"Therefore, we are utterly exhausted and emaciated by our ascetic penance."
Then an incorporeal being dwelling in the sky said something to them:
"O men, you have seen the white ones."
They are devoid of all sense faculties. O Lord of Gods, when these [deities] are seen, the best of the twice-born are likewise seen.
"Go now, all you sages, back whence you came from here without delay;
he cannot be reached by one who lacks devotion."
The Lord can somehow be seen at all only by those who have attained single-minded devotion over a long period of time.
That Blessed One can be seen,
though his halo of light makes him difficult to behold;
yet, a great task must be accomplished.
O best of the twice-born,
when this Kṛta Yuga has passed away and even when the reversal of the ages has occurred, you [shall remain].
When the Tretā Yuga had arrived during the Vaivasvata interval, O brahmins,
[he appeared] for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
"You shall indeed become my companions.
Then, O Soma-drinkers, having heard those wonderful words, they were thus [addressed].
"By his grace, we have swiftly reached this desired region;
thus it was through our great asceticism."
"Even though we have offered oblations to the gods and the ancestors,
that deity has not been seen by us;
how then are you able to see him?"
Nārāyaṇa is the Great Being,
the creator of the universe, and the consumer of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings.
Without beginning or end, unmanifest,
and worshipped by gods and demons.
